title: Why Schools Are Rolling Back Productive Struggle
author: Holly Korbey
source: The Bell Ringer (Holly Korbey Substack), May 1, 2026
summary: Korbey reports on a growing rejection of 'productive struggle' as the default teaching frame in elementary math, where students are asked to attempt problems before being shown how. Following the structured-literacy turn, teachers like Daniel Carr in Oregon and Takia McClendon in Philadelphia have found that the popular sequence (try first, then teach) leaves novices frustrated while only the few who already knew how succeed. Drawing on the instructional hierarchy from behavioural psychology, the article argues that acquisition requires explicit step-by-step instruction first, then guided practice, then transfer to new problems, in that order. State and district leaders in Texas and Arlington Virginia are refining guidance and adopting evidence-aligned materials, while researchers like Ben Solomon and curriculum architects like William McCallum push back on the misinterpretation that students should figure everything out on their own. The piece pairs research evidence with classroom outcomes: McClendon's class moved from 15 to 71 percent fluency; Carr's class jumped from 33 to 52 percent passing the Smarter Balanced assessment after he switched to explicit instruction first.
points: Popular elementary math curricula (i-Ready, Go Math, Building Thinking Classrooms) embed a try-first-teach-later sequence that leaves novices to fail at problems they have not been taught to solve.

The instructional hierarchy from behavioural psychology orders learning as acquisition (explicit step-by-step instruction), then fluency (practice), then generalisation (transfer to new problems); productive struggle inverts this for novices.

Fact fluency reduces working-memory load and makes new problems tractable; many state standards and curricula assume fluency will emerge from problem solving rather than be built through deliberate practice.

Singapore's open-ended math problems work because students arrive at school already fluent in basic arithmetic (often via two hours of after-school tutoring), a context American adopters routinely miss.

Districts that paired structured-literacy success with a math reassessment (Arlington VA, Texas) are adopting evidence-aligned materials, and individual teachers who add deliberate fluency practice see measurable gains (15 to 71 percent fluency in one Philadelphia classroom; 33 to 52 percent state-test pass rate in one Oregon class).
quotes: A survey conducted by the teachers' union found that nine out of ten teachers said their students were 'confused, off-task, or unable to begin,' because of the way math lessons were arranged.

Many of the most popular elementary school math curricula, as well as how teachers are shown to think about math, have students try to solve an unknown math problem first, then have the teacher come in later to guide students through the steps of how to solve it.

Some people have interpreted problem-based instruction as if the students should figure out everything on their own. That's not what I believe. It's not what the standards say. It's not in the IM curriculum, and it's not good teaching.

I have kids who know how to do the math, but they're making mistakes on just doing long division. They don't know their subtraction facts. When I take a look at the bottom of your page, and you're drawing tally marks, because when you got to the subtraction part, that's the only way you know how to do it.

When a student is brand-new to an idea, when they're in the acquisition stage, then they need explicit, step-by-step instruction so they can have a 'correct and complete understanding' of what they're trying to do. As they become more fluent, the teaching tactics can change, first to practice problems, and then finally, at the end of mastering a concept, applying knowledge to new problems.
We saw very strong growth in reading. While at the same time we saw math, especially for the least advantaged kids, the growth was just not matching up.

I saw that this was totally solvable. I started implementing research, the science of learning principles in my classroom, and had the highest state test scores I've ever had.” Archived from The Bell Ringer (Holly Korbey Substack) on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
